newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Death rate drops in world's murder capital.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Death rate drops in world's murder capital.

text.p: This city in northwest Colombia has a longtime reputation as the world's murder capital and its chief medical examiner still has his hands full, but the number of killings has dropped since 1991.

Even as the medical examiner, Dr. Cesar Augusto Giraldo, and other residents confront levels of violence that would be considered intolerable elsewhere, he sees hope that the worst of Medellin's bloodletting is over.

Doctors performing triage in the emergency room of the city's main hospital, San Vicente de Paul, are still inundated by about 140 patients a day, some 60 percent of them victims of gunshot or stab wounds or some other violent trauma. But that is down from 70 or 80 percent in the recent past and Giraldo, an epidemiologist, said the overall trend is toward a decline in Medellin's "contagion of violence."

"There's still a lot of violence among us," he conceded in an interview with Reuters. "But the worst is over ... I truly hope, looking at the statistics and holding death here in my hands, that we're going to see better days."

Giraldo, medical examiner since 1974, can remember times at the height of Medellin's violence when his office had to perform autopsies on as many as 30 murder victims a day. His job is less overwhelming now but he is still one of the busiest coroners on Earth.

The National Police reported 5,257 homicides in the Medellin metropolitan area last year alone, an average of more than 14 a day in an area with a population of less than three million. Bogota, with more than twice as many residents, was well behind Medellin with a total of 2,708 murders in 1996.

Giraldo's office said the toll amounted to a total of 239 violent deaths in Medellin proper for every 100,000 residents last year, down from 248 in 1995 and 292 in 1994. The worst violence this decade was in 1991, when Medellin saw 400 violent deaths for every 100,000 residents.

Despite the drop, Giraldo said, the city remains the world's most violent by far. He cited a recent study by Sao Paulo's Pontificia Universidad Catolica as saying Johannesburg ranked as the world's second most violent urban area -- but with a murder rate less than half that of Medellin.

"Violentologos," academics devoted to the study of violent crime, say a whole catalogue of problems lies behind violence in Medellin and elsewhere in Colombia including grinding poverty, gang-related vendettas and the drug trade once controlled with a vengeance by Medellin's own Pablo Escobar.

Human rights officials also cite a surge in political killings in Medellin as rightist gunmen target some of the more than 45,000 peasants and suspected rebel sympathisers who have poured into the city's teeming slums in the past year to escape the guerrilla war bleeding the countryside.
IMPUNITY, LACK OF INFORMATION ADD TO CRIME

Giraldo said impunity for killers, and the fact that there was no information on motives behind nearly 90 percent of the homicides he dealt with last year, were factors clearly contributing to violent crime.
But the proliferation of guns in the city, mixed with a high level of dependency on over-the-counter drugs and alcohol, were the true driving forces behind the "social disease" of violence, he said.

"This is a crime of the developed countries ... It's white- collar crime," he said of potent tranquillisers and pain killers that he alleged multinational drug companies were dumping on Latin America without restrictions or appropriate warning labels required in Europe and the United States.
"Instead of destroying them they're selling them to us," he added, saying drugs and drug-related dementia were at the bottom of countless killings in Medellin.

On the issue of firearms, which remain the leading cause of death in Medellin, Mayor Sergio Naranjo told Reuters more than 100,000 guns and knives had been confiscated in the past year as police moved to enforce a ban on carrying weapons within the city limits.
But one police official said the 100,000 was just "the tip of the iceberg," adding: "Most people in this city are still armed to the teeth."
